headlines: The 2-year yield is 4.81% and is up 74 bp over 13 weeks; the 10-year is 5.17% and is up 79 bp.
The 2-year yield rose 47 bp in the last 4 weeks, larger than 93% of 4-week moves since 1990: an unusually quick repricing of where markets expect the Federal Reserve to take rates.
The 10-year yield rose 44 bp in the last 4 weeks, larger than 92% of 4-week moves since 1990: an unusually quick repricing of long-term borrowing costs, including mortgage rates.
The 10-year pays 0.36 percentage points more than the 2-year, so the curve is not inverted; it has been positive since September 2024.
Compared with the same period last year: Taiwan 46% higher; Korea 78% higher; Japan 19% higher (11% in U.S. dollars).

panels.title: Interest rates and the yield curve
panels.explainer: The 2-year yield tracks where the bond market expects the Federal Reserve's rate to be over the next two years. The 10-year reflects long-run growth and inflation expectations. When the gap between them turns negative (an inverted curve), the market expects rate cuts, usually because it expects a slowdown. Inversions have come before most U.S. recessions of the past 50 years, with lead times from months to about two years, and some false alarms.
takeaway: The 2-year yield is 4.81% and is up 74 bp over 13 weeks; the 10-year is 5.17% and is up 79 bp.
The 2-year yield rose 47 bp in the last 4 weeks, larger than 93% of 4-week moves since 1990: an unusually quick repricing of where markets expect the Federal Reserve to take rates.
The 10-year yield rose 44 bp in the last 4 weeks, larger than 92% of 4-week moves since 1990: an unusually quick repricing of long-term borrowing costs, including mortgage rates.
The 10-year pays 0.36 percentage points more than the 2-year, so the curve is not inverted; it has been positive since September 2024.
The shape of the curve barely changed over 13 weeks.

panels.title: Positioning: what hedge funds are doing
panels.explainer: Big banks' prime-brokerage desks lend to hedge funds and see their trades. Their notes go to clients first and reach Reuters, the FT, Barron's and others days later. This strip counts those stories and shows the newest; it measures how much the press is talking about positioning, not the positions themselves.
